distillation_scope.leaf_granularity: First-layer clinical disease leaf for pulmonary embolism across acute thrombotic pulmonary arterial obstruction. Massive, intermediate-risk, low-risk, provoked, unprovoked, recurrent, pregnancy-associated, cancer-associated, catheter-associated, fat, air, septic, tumor embolism, and chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension contexts are represented as risk, context, event, treatment-modifier, or future subtype axes rather than disease-name qualifiers.
distillation_scope.ranking_note: Presentation ranking may consume symptoms, vitals, gas exchange, D-dimer, cardiac strain biomarkers, ECG/echo/duplex/CTPA/VQ evidence, and initial pulmonary infarction or pleural findings when those data are available at the chosen evidence stage. Final diagnosis, thrombophilia workup, long-term outcome, clot resolution, and treatment response remain confirmatory or non-ranking unless a separate post-workup mode explicitly consumes them.

latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Deep venous or right-heart thrombus forms under venous stasis, endothelial injury, hypercoagulability, malignancy, estrogen/pregnancy, inflammatory, catheter, or inherited/acquired thrombophilia contexts.
Thrombus embolizes to one or more pulmonary arteries, creating anatomic filling defects and reducing perfusion in affected vascular beds.
Perfusion obstruction creates dead-space ventilation, regional hypoperfusion, tachypnea, respiratory alkalosis, hypoxemia, dyspnea, and respiratory distress in susceptible patients.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Pulmonary vascular resistance and right-ventricular afterload
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Mechanical obstruction, hypoxic vasoconstriction, and vasoactive mediators raise pulmonary vascular resistance and acutely increase right-ventricular afterload.
Acute right-ventricular pressure overload can produce dilation, septal shift, reduced left-sided filling, hypotension, syncope, obstructive shock, cardiac arrest, and death.
Distal emboli with impaired collateral flow can cause infarction, pleuritic pain, hemoptysis, small pleural effusion, and wedge-shaped peripheral opacity.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Fibrinolysis and cardiac strain biomarker response
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Fibrin turnover raises D-dimer while right-ventricular stretch and ischemia can raise BNP/NT-proBNP and troponin in proportion to strain and reserve.
Persistent thrombus, recurrent embolization, and organized vascular obstruction can create recurrent VTE hazard or later chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Many pulmonary emboli arise from clinically or sonographically apparent lower-extremity DVT.
Symptomatic leg pain or swelling can accompany the source DVT.
Venous thrombus can detach and embolize to the pulmonary arterial tree.
Pulmonary arterial thrombus is visualized as an intraluminal contrast filling defect on CTPA.
More occluded vascular beds produce higher observed embolic burden.
Central clot location is one possible expression of pulmonary arterial occlusion.
Segmental or subsegmental clot location is another possible expression of pulmonary arterial occlusion.
Perfusion defects with preserved ventilation create V/Q mismatch.
Vascular obstruction is the upstream driver of dead-space ventilation and hypoxemia.
Dead-space ventilation and hypoxemia commonly manifest as dyspnea.
Severe gas-exchange strain can produce visible respiratory distress.
Hypoxemia lowers pulse oximetry, though saturation may be normal in smaller or compensated PE.
Tachypnea is a frequent physiologic response to dead-space ventilation.
Hyperventilation commonly lowers PaCO2.
Respiratory alkalosis can occur early from hyperventilation.
Occluded pulmonary vascular beds acutely raise pulmonary vascular resistance.
Acute afterload elevation can be seen as elevated pulmonary pressure on echo.
Right-ventricular pressure overload causes dilation.
RV afterload produces echocardiographic or CT signs of RV strain.
RV pressure overload can flatten or bow the septum toward the LV.
Severe RV afterload can outstrip RV reserve and reduce LV preload.
Low cardiac output and obstructive shock lower systolic pressure.
Obstructive shock lowers MAP.
Tachycardia reflects adrenergic compensation and RV strain.
Transient low cerebral perfusion or arrhythmia can cause syncope.
RV failure is the core pathway into PE-related obstructive shock.
Extreme RV failure can deteriorate into pulseless electrical activity or arrest.
Low-output shock increases lactate.
Pulmonary infarction and pleural irritation can produce chest pain.
PE chest pain is often pleuritic when peripheral infarction or pleural irritation is present.
Peripheral infarction can cause hemoptysis.
Infarction can become visible as wedge-shaped opacity or parenchymal infarct.
Small pleural effusions commonly accompany PE or infarction.
Cross-linked fibrin breakdown raises D-dimer, though small, delayed, or already treated PE can have low values.
RV strain and ischemia can raise troponin.
RV stretch can raise BNP.
Ongoing hypercoagulability or inadequate anticoagulation increases recurrence risk.
Organized unresolved thrombus can produce chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension.
PE-related obstructive shock is a major immediate mortality pathway.
Cardiac arrest from PE carries high short-term mortality.
Respiratory failure worsens survival in PE, especially with limited cardiopulmonary reserve.
Major anticoagulation- or thrombolysis-associated bleeding can be fatal or force undertreatment.

axes.shape_free_text: Subjective dyspnea or shortness of breath from V/Q mismatch, hypoxemia, or RV strain; can be absent in atypical PE.
Visible respiratory distress, increased work of breathing, or severe air hunger.
Chest pain from pleural irritation, pulmonary infarction, RV ischemia, or nonspecific cardiopulmonary strain.
Pain worsened by inspiration or cough, reflecting peripheral infarction or pleural inflammation.
Hemoptysis from pulmonary infarction or hemorrhagic peripheral embolic injury; absent in many PE cases.
Syncope from transient obstructive shock, arrhythmia, or severe RV outflow limitation.
Near-syncope, lightheadedness, or collapse tendency from PE-related low output.
Calf or leg pain, swelling, or tenderness suggesting source venous thrombosis.
Heart rate; tachycardia can reflect PE, hypoxemia, pain, or shock.
Respiratory rate; tachypnea is common but may be absent.
Pulse oximetry oxygen saturation; ranges from normal to severely low depending on embolic burden and reserve.
Systolic blood pressure; may be normal or low with obstructive shock.
Mean arterial pressure; low values mark obstructive shock physiology.
Body temperature; PE can be afebrile or cause low-grade fever, but high fever suggests competing infection/inflammation.
D-dimer from fibrin turnover; often elevated but can be low in small, delayed, anticoagulated, or atypical cases.
Arterial oxygen tension; low with hypoxemia but can be near normal.
Arterial carbon dioxide tension; often low from hyperventilation and may rise in fatigue or severe comorbidity.
Arterial pH; respiratory alkalosis can raise pH early, while shock acidosis may lower it.
Troponin as RV strain or ischemia marker; can be normal in low-risk PE and high with RV injury or competing ACS.
BNP as a marker of ventricular stretch in RV strain; baseline is affected by age, renal function, and chronic heart disease.
Lactate rises with PE-related shock or tissue hypoperfusion.
CT pulmonary angiography evidence of pulmonary arterial intraluminal filling defects.
Overall anatomic thrombus burden across main, lobar, segmental, and subsegmental pulmonary arteries.
Main pulmonary artery, right/left pulmonary artery, central, or saddle embolic involvement.
Segmental or subsegmental pulmonary artery embolic involvement.
V/Q mismatch or perfusion defect consistent with pulmonary vascular obstruction.
Pulmonary infarction, Hampton-hump-like wedge opacity, or peripheral infarct pattern downstream of embolic occlusion.
Pleural effusion present on imaging; PE-associated effusions are often small and may be ipsilateral, contralateral, or migratory.
Compression ultrasound, duplex, or clinical evidence of lower-extremity deep venous thrombosis; absence does not exclude PE.
Venous thrombosis in proximal leg, distal calf, pelvic, catheter, or right-heart sources.
Echocardiographic or CT pattern of acute RV strain, including McConnell sign, reduced RV systolic function, septal shift, or RV/LV enlargement.
Right ventricular or right atrial dilation from acute pressure overload.
Septal flattening or leftward septal shift from RV pressure overload.
Elevated pulmonary artery pressure on echo or catheter data during PE or chronic thromboembolic disease.
Right-heart thrombus in transit or intracardiac thrombus visualized by echocardiography or CT.
Daily hazard of PE-related obstructive shock from RV failure and low LV filling.
Daily hazard of PE-related cardiac arrest, often pulseless electrical activity or sudden collapse.
Daily hazard of respiratory failure requiring high-flow oxygen, noninvasive ventilation, intubation, or ECMO.
Daily hazard of recurrent DVT or PE under persistent risk, inadequate anticoagulation, or high thrombotic burden.
Daily hazard of later chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension after unresolved or recurrent embolic obstruction.
Daily hazard of clinically important bleeding from anticoagulation, thrombolysis, invasive catheter therapy, trauma, coagulopathy, thrombocytopenia, or active bleeding lesions.
Daily hazard of intracranial hemorrhage, especially under thrombolysis, anticoagulation, recent stroke, trauma, hypertension, or intracranial lesions.
Daily hazard of clinically important bleeding from catheter access, surgical embolectomy, ECMO cannulation, vascular injury, or periprocedural anticoagulation.
Context probability that therapeutic anticoagulation can be given without prohibitive active bleeding or procedure constraint.
Context probability of major bleeding or contraindication relevant to systemic or catheter-directed thrombolysis.
Renal dysfunction context that affects CTPA contrast use, LMWH/DOAC dosing, and bleeding risk.

Lifespan outcome hazard for D-PULMONARY-EMBOLISM, driven by obstructive shock, cardiac arrest, refractory hypoxemia, severe comorbidity, recurrence, and treatment-limiting bleeding. Not a separate death manifold.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: DVT and PE often coexist, but absence of visible DVT does not exclude PE.
Higher embolic burden tends to raise RV afterload and strain.
Central clot location raises risk of hemodynamic compromise, though shock also depends on reserve.
Troponin tends to rise when RV strain is substantial.
BNP tends to rise with RV stretch.
RV dilation and septal flattening often appear together under pressure overload.
Severe RV strain can transition into obstructive shock.
Untreated or refractory obstructive shock can deteriorate into arrest.
Lower saturation often increases respiratory distress, though dyspnea can occur with normal saturation.
Hyperventilation lowers PaCO2 unless fatigue or chronic lung disease intervenes.
Peripheral infarction can irritate pleura and cause inspiratory pain.
Pulmonary infarction and inflammatory mediator release can produce small effusions.
D-dimer tends to rise with thrombus burden but is nonspecific and can be normal in selected cases.
Inability to anticoagulate increases recurrent VTE risk.
Global major bleeding hazard includes transition to intracranial hemorrhage under thrombolysis or anticoagulation.
Major bleeding can directly kill or limit PE therapy.
Shock is the dominant acute PE mortality pathway.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Active major bleeding or urgent procedure may prevent therapeutic anticoagulation.
Heparin adds bleeding risk when baseline bleeding hazard is high.

treatments.clinical_rationale: Rapidly titratable anticoagulation limits clot propagation and recurrence and is useful when procedures, instability, renal dysfunction, or rapid reversal are relevant.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Renal dysfunction changes accumulation and dosing safety.
High bleeding hazard narrows usable anticoagulant intensity.

treatments.clinical_rationale: Parenteral anticoagulation limits propagation and recurrence when renal function and bleeding context permit.

treatments.display_name: Direct oral anticoagulant for pulmonary embolism

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Renal dysfunction and drug interactions can constrain DOAC use.
Bleeding risk affects anticoagulant selection and intensity.

treatments.clinical_rationale: Oral factor Xa or thrombin inhibition suppresses recurrence risk after acute PE when the patient can absorb and safely receive it.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Over-anticoagulation or labile INR raises bleeding risk.

treatments.clinical_rationale: Longer-term anticoagulation option when monitoring, interactions, pregnancy context, renal context, cost, or antiphospholipid context make it coherent.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: The hemodynamic benefit is most consequential when shock hazard is high.
Recent stroke, intracranial lesion, trauma, surgery, or active bleeding can dominate net effect.

treatments.clinical_rationale: Systemic fibrinolysis rapidly reduces thrombus burden and RV afterload, with benefit and harm determined by shock physiology and bleeding context.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Bleeding risk can favor mechanical thrombectomy or lower local lytic exposure over systemic lysis.
Access-site and lytic-related bleeding remain relevant.

side_effects.interpretation: Vascular access or catheter complication risk

treatments.clinical_rationale: Endovascular reperfusion can reduce clot burden and RV strain when anatomy, expertise, and bleeding context make it coherent.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Surgery may remain a reperfusion option when lysis risk is prohibitive and surgical resources are available.

treatments.clinical_rationale: Operative embolectomy mechanically removes obstructing clot when anatomy and patient context support surgical reperfusion.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Filter benefit is most coherent when anticoagulation cannot be used or recurrent embolization occurs despite it.

side_effects.interpretation: Filter-associated thrombosis or DVT propagation risk

treatments.clinical_rationale: A caval filter can reduce embolization from lower-extremity clot in selected anticoagulation-limited contexts but does not dissolve existing pulmonary thrombus.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Oxygen improves hypoxemia but does not remove pulmonary vascular obstruction.

treatments.clinical_rationale: Supplemental oxygen raises arterial oxygen content while definitive clot-directed therapy acts on the embolic field.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Pressors support perfusion but cannot remove obstruction.

treatments.clinical_rationale: Vasopressors support coronary and systemic perfusion during PE-related obstructive shock while reperfusion or anticoagulation addresses the cause.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Positive pressure can reduce venous return and worsen RV loading if not managed carefully.

side_effects.interpretation: Positive pressure may worsen preload and blood pressure in RV failure

treatments.clinical_rationale: Ventilatory support treats respiratory failure but must be balanced against RV preload and pressure effects.

treatments.display_name: ECMO bridge for refractory PE shock

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Cannulation and circuit anticoagulation increase bleeding risk.

treatments.clinical_rationale: Mechanical circulatory support can bridge refractory shock or arrest to reperfusion, anticoagulation, or recovery when resources and bleeding context allow.

risk_factors.display_name: Recent surgery, trauma, hospitalization, or immobility

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Stasis and endothelial injury raise source DVT likelihood.
Recent surgery or trauma can limit anticoagulation or thrombolysis.
Postoperative or traumatic bleeding context increases treatment bleeding risk.
Cancer-associated thrombosis increases recurrence risk.
Tumor bleeding, thrombocytopenia, procedures, and drug interactions can increase bleeding.

risk_factors.display_name: Pregnancy, postpartum, or estrogen exposure context

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Pregnancy and estrogenic contexts promote VTE.
Pregnancy changes imaging and anticoagulant selection context.
Prior VTE and thrombophilia increase recurrence hazard.
Baseline inflammatory or thrombotic context can alter D-dimer interpretation.
Baseline dyspnea can be high and PE presentation less specific.
Underlying lung or heart disease lowers reserve.
Reduced RV or pulmonary reserve increases hemodynamic risk for a given embolic burden.
Frailty and cardiopulmonary disease worsen survival.
Renal impairment affects contrast imaging and anticoagulant choice.
Renal dysfunction can raise BNP independent of acute RV strain.
Renal dysfunction increases anticoagulant accumulation and bleeding risk.

risk_factors.display_name: Active bleeding, recent stroke, trauma, or intracranial lesion context

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Bleeding or CNS risk can preclude anticoagulation.
Thrombolysis harm rises with active or recent bleeding-risk contexts.
Intracranial risk factors strongly increase ICH hazard under lysis or anticoagulation.
Older age worsens PE reserve and bleeding risk.
Age increases anticoagulation and thrombolysis bleeding hazard.
Young patients usually have greater cardiopulmonary reserve if clot burden is not massive.

supportive_care.description: Track blood pressure, heart rate, oxygen saturation, respiratory rate, urine output, lactate, and clinical work of breathing during acute PE.
Use echo/CT RV strain, troponin/BNP, shock markers, clot burden, and bleeding-risk context as state axes rather than fixed treatment labels.
Balance oxygenation, preload, vasopressors, and ventilation carefully when RV failure is active.
Assess lower-extremity/pelvic/catheter thrombosis and ongoing hypercoagulable context to inform recurrence hazard.
After acute stabilization, reassess provoking context, bleeding risk, recurrence risk, symptoms, and evidence of chronic thromboembolic disease.

ontology_notes: Pulmonary embolism here is the first-layer disease leaf. Massive, submassive, provoked, unprovoked, recurrent, and chronic thromboembolic contexts are not encoded in the disease name.
CTPA, V/Q, echo, duplex, and D-dimer evidence may be rankable when the case is explicitly a post-imaging or post-lab evidence-stage test; final diagnosis and response to therapy remain non-ranking.
Anticoagulation and thrombolysis effects are represented through recurrent VTE, embolic burden, RV strain, shock, major bleeding, ICH, and mortality hazards rather than treatment labels.
